video_title: Michael Howell: FED Rate Hikes Will Trigger The Biggest Bull Run Ever
gist: Michael Howell (Capital Wars) argues the West's debt overhang has turned financial markets into pure debt-refinancing engines, forcing governments to fund themselves at the short end (quasi money-printing) and keeping gold and Bitcoin as the key monetary-inflation hedges, even as equities face looming PE-multiple compression and 10-year yields push toward 6%.

themes.theme: Debt refinancing regime & no path to austerity

insights.claim: Financial markets have structurally shifted from being new-capital-raising mechanisms to debt-refinancing engines, with roughly 80% of all primary transactions in global capital markets now being debt refinancing rather than funding new investment.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: In a refinancing-dominated market, balance-sheet/liquidity capacity to roll over debt matters more than the cost of capital (interest rates) when forecasting asset prices.
insights.quote: We would reckon that about 80% of all primary transactions in capital markets worldwide are now debt refinancing transactions.

insights.claim: US public debt has grown roughly 12x since year 2000, and the federal government is running a persistent fiscal deficit of about 6% of GDP with no sign of narrowing.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: A structurally compounding deficit reinforces the case for long-run currency debasement and hard-asset allocation over cash and long bonds.
insights.quote: public public debt is probably something like uh what 12 times bigger than it was in uh uh in year 2000

insights.claim: Aging demographics across the West combined with an escalating US-China 'capital war' over dollar-versus-yuan dominance make austerity politically and strategically impossible, and Howell warns that competition could eventually morph into military conflict, meaning governments will keep spending and financing deficits through money creation rather than tax hikes or cuts.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Removes austerity as a realistic policy path and flags great-power conflict as a tail risk, both of which argue for holding monetary-inflation and geopolitical hedges (gold, crypto) over long-duration bonds.
insights.quote: those capital wars for example between the US and China uh for the dominance of um of um the dollar or the yuan system uh in the long term that is likely to morph into maybe military conflict at some stage

themes.theme: Monetary inflation as the master mechanism

insights.claim: Governments, led by the US, are increasingly funding themselves with short-dated 3-6 month Treasury bills rather than long bonds; this now makes up about a quarter of total debt issuance and is set to grow toward a third, which Howell treats as a quasi money-printing mechanism because banks buy the bills and expand their balance sheets and the broader money supply.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: The rising share of short-bill issuance is a trackable leading indicator of accelerating monetary inflation, ahead of any change in headline policy rates.
insights.quote: that percentage of debt issuance which is currently about a quarter of total debt issuance is now in in this short-term these short-term instruments it's going to grow to probably a third

insights.claim: Howell argues the real story is 'monetary inflation' (currency debasement that erodes the wealth of anyone not holding inflation-hedge assets), not 'financial repression' as commonly framed by the media, and that main-street inflation and monetary inflation are distinct but related destructive forces.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Reframes the debt/inflation debate: the losers are savers in non-hedge assets, not just consumers facing CPI, which argues for actively rotating into gold/crypto rather than assuming standard inflation protection (e.g., TIPS) is sufficient.
insights.quote: we've argued that, you know, it's slightly misguided to talk about financial repression. That's not really the the full story. The full story is you're getting monetary inflation.

insights.claim: Over the past 10 years, Bitcoin has shown roughly a 10x multiplier to global liquidity changes -- a 10% increase in global liquidity has corresponded to roughly a doubling of Bitcoin's price -- meaning only a small portfolio allocation (a few percent) is needed for meaningful monetary-inflation-hedge protection.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Investors can treat a small (3-4%) Bitcoin allocation as an efficient, leveraged liquidity/inflation hedge rather than needing a large position to move portfolio outcomes.
insights.quote: for every 10% increase in global liquidity, you get something like a a doubling of the Bitcoin price

insights.claim: Howell's global liquidity sensitivity ranking places crypto (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana) and precious metals (gold, silver) at the high-sensitivity end, while long-duration fixed income -- the yield curve and 10-year US Treasuries -- is negatively correlated to global liquidity, meaning bonds tend to fall in value precisely when liquidity is expanding.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Provides a ranked hedge list investors can use to reposition portfolios ahead of anticipated liquidity-regime shifts, overweighting crypto/precious metals and underweighting long bonds.

themes.theme: The debt-liquidity cycle: framework and indicators

insights.claim: Howell's 'debt-liquidity cycle' framework holds that debt requires liquidity to be refinanced while liquidity requires good-quality debt as collateral (roughly 80% of total liquidity creation is collateral-backed via repo); when the two become mismatched -- too much debt to refinance versus available liquidity -- the debt-liquidity ratio spikes, the system fails into a refinancing crisis, and central banks are forced to intervene because new credit structurally rests on old debt not being allowed to default.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: A rising debt-to-liquidity ratio is an early-warning signal for financial crisis and imminent central-bank money printing -- worth tracking as a systemic-risk gauge.
insights.quote: debt needs liquidity for refinancing but equally liquidity needs good quality debt as collateral... central banks come in and support the system. They simply have to otherwise the system would fail.

insights.claim: Howell says the key indicators for monitoring repo and collateral market stability are the SOFR-to-Fed-funds spread, the MOVE index (bond market volatility), and the term premium in bond markets, which is most easily proxied by watching the slope of the yield curve -- not headline policy interest rates.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete, trackable dashboard for anticipating liquidity stress ahead of, and instead of, headline Fed rate decisions.
insights.quote: the first indicator is to look at the repo markets uh and to look at what sofa spreads are. The second thing to look at is uh to look at uh bond volatility through the move index.

insights.claim: Howell dismisses the popular 'four-year Bitcoin halving cycle' narrative, arguing the real driver of crypto cycles is a five-to-six-year debt-refinancing/liquidity cycle, implying traders waiting for a seasonal October bottom based on the four-year cycle model may be using the wrong framework and could be left behind.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Investors timing crypto entries around halving-based four-year cycle models should instead track the debt-refinancing calendar and liquidity indicators per Howell's framework.
insights.quote: there's there's no there's no four-year cycle as far as we can see. I mean the cycle is different. the cycle is more like a refinancing cycle based around debt which is a five to six year cycle.

themes.theme: Bessent/Fed liquidity signaling and the rate-hike paradox

insights.claim: Howell says the market and media misread Treasury Secretary Bessent's move to double Treasury bond buybacks -- buybacks are too small to meaningfully influence yields -- arguing the real purpose is to suppress bond market volatility (the MOVE index) and keep the bond market orderly.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Treasury buyback announcements should be read as volatility-suppression signals, not yield-management tools, when assessing their market impact.
insights.quote: I think that what I mean I think the media in in many cases misread that Bessant move... What he's trying to influence is volatility in the market.

insights.claim: Fed Chair Walsh's FOMC pledge to keep bank reserves at 'ample' levels is, per Howell, a signal aimed at keeping money markets and repo funding liquid and stable, working in tandem with Bessent's Treasury actions to jointly control collateral stability and repo liquidity.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Statements about bank reserve adequacy are a policy lever worth monitoring as closely as rate decisions, since they directly target the repo/collateral stability Howell says actually drives markets.
insights.quote: one of the things that they intended to do was to keep uh bank reserves uh at uh adequate or ample levels

insights.claim: Howell attributes Bitcoin's breakout to roughly $80,000 directly to the combined Bessent/Fed liquidity signals, viewing the rally as market confirmation that policymakers intend to keep funding the government at the short end and maintain ample system liquidity.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Treasury/Fed liquidity-signaling events (buybacks, reserve-level guidance) can function as tradeable leading catalysts for crypto and gold rallies.
insights.quote: my view is that crypto and gold took that as a cue and that's why they took off.

insights.claim: Howell argues rate hikes in the current regime could be stimulative rather than contractionary: because the government is now a huge net borrower, a higher policy rate increases the interest income transferred to the private sector holding government debt, and he expects a 25bp hike could even cause long-end Treasury yields to rally as markets read it as reassurance the Fed is being disciplined -- the opposite of the mainstream media's expected reaction.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Investors shouldn't assume a hawkish Fed move is automatically bearish for risk assets or bonds in a high-debt regime; a hike could paradoxically ease bond-market stress.
insights.quote: if you increase interest rates in the US, you're actually giving the private sector more cash. Well, that's a stimulus, not not a not a contraction.

insights.claim: Fed Chair Walsh reviving M2/money-supply growth as an explicit part of the monetary policy framework, after decades of it being dropped, is per Howell a face-saving pivot that effectively buys the Fed one-to-three years before the monetary aggregates start signaling serious trouble.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: M2 growth reappearing in Fed communications is itself a signal worth tracking as an admission that liquidity, not just rates, is now central to policy -- and a marker for how much runway remains before trouble surfaces.
insights.quote: it may well be uh one, two, three years before the monetary aggregates really start to spell trouble. And that means they're buying time.

themes.theme: China, PBOC liquidity and the gold/crypto link

insights.claim: Howell argues the primary catalyst for gold's rally was not the Russia-Ukraine war but the People's Bank of China printing money to manage what he calls the largest debt burden of any major economy.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: PBOC liquidity data may be a better leading indicator for gold price direction than geopolitical headlines, and is worth tracking directly rather than inferring gold moves from war news.
insights.quote: contrary to what many commentators argue that the gold market, uh, catapulted higher after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, actually the key catalyst was the People's Bank of China printing money.

insights.claim: Because China bans crypto trading, capital responding to Chinese monetary debasement flows mainly into gold, but Howell's Capital Wars research found PBOC liquidity still has a measurable, likely indirect effect on crypto prices, probably spilling over via the real economy and the gold market.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: PBOC liquidity is a global cross-asset variable worth including in crypto price models even though China formally excludes crypto from its financial system.
insights.quote: the People's Bank of China has a big impact on the crypto markets too... it's having a big effect, too.

insights.claim: Howell believes the 'great debasement' has not yet happened in the West -- current gold strength is being driven primarily by Chinese monetary inflation -- implying Western currency debasement is still to come as an additional future tailwind for gold and crypto.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: If correct, the current gold/crypto rally driven by China is only a preview -- a later, larger Western debasement wave would be a further catalyst investors should watch for.
insights.quote: You haven't really had the great debasement in the west yet. That's coming. Okay, that's that's cream on top, right?

themes.theme: Equities and the AI bubble parallel

insights.claim: Howell expects equity indices to underperform going forward: as bond yields rise and liquidity leaves the financial sector for the real economy, PE multiples come under downward pressure even as earnings still grow for now, and he projects weaker earnings growth alongside further multiple contraction materializing around 2027.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Suggests a fading equity cycle into 2027 -- investors should watch for the earnings/PE inflection point rather than assuming the current earnings strength persists.
insights.quote: what you'd expect to see is in 2027, you'd expect to see weaker earnings growth. Um, and you'd expect to see a P multiple that probably contracts

insights.claim: Howell admits his prior call that Wall Street would be rangebound this year was wrong, because real economic strength delivered a much bigger earnings surprise than he expected, which kept PE multiples elevated despite rising bond yields.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: A candid track-record admission -- signals that the earnings side of the equity equation has so far outrun the liquidity/yield headwind he expected, which is itself a data point on model reliability.
insights.quote: we've been surprised by the E number uh and we've been surprised as well by the fact that PE have held up.

insights.claim: Howell's standing recommended trade has been to 'top slice' equity gains and rotate into commodities, which he says has worked well so far this cycle.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable rotation trade: trim equity winners and add commodity exposure as the liquidity cycle matures and real-economy strength persists.
insights.quote: we've been saying to people top slice and go into commodities. Uh, that's been a good trade clearly.

insights.claim: Howell compares the current AI investment boom to the late-1990s fiber-optic bubble exemplified by Global Crossing -- then the market darling, likened to today's Nvidia -- which went into Chapter 11 within about five years as margins collapsed under competition; he says he believes in AI as a technology but not necessarily in the current valuations of specific AI companies given fierce competition from both US rivals and Chinese players.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Flags AI infrastructure names as vulnerable to the same margin-compression/bankruptcy pattern seen in the dot-com-era fiber buildout, even though the underlying technology (like fiber optics) may persist and prove valuable long-term.
insights.quote: global crossing isn't. It went into chapter 11 sort of within 5 years and that's the nature of capitalism... I'm a great believer in AI. Whether I'm a great believer in specific AI companies is a different question.

themes.theme: Bond market outlook and portfolio math

insights.claim: Howell projects 10-year US Treasury yields will test 6% and possibly go higher, based on current nominal GDP growth of roughly 7-8% (a level last seen in the mid-1980s, when bond yields were around 8%) and the expectation that yields converge toward nominal growth rates.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: A specific, falsifiable level (6% on the 10-year) to watch for confirming or rejecting the higher-for-longer bond yield thesis.
insights.quote: I would fully expect yields at the 10-year uh tenor in the US to test 6% uh in the you know in the foreseeable future um and possibly go higher.

insights.claim: A COVID-era 'debt maturity wall' -- debt that was refinanced out to the later 2020s during the pandemic -- is now coming due in the next few years, adding a major additional refinancing load on top of ongoing deficit financing, which will require central banks to keep money-market liquidity ample.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete forward catalyst and rough timeline for renewed liquidity injections -- worth tracking upcoming Treasury and corporate refinancing calendars for the late 2020s.
insights.quote: there was a lot of debt then that was refinanced uh to the later years of this decade uh the so-called debt maturity wall which is coming back uh in the next few years

insights.claim: Howell frames bond investing as a straightforward math exercise: at a 5% starting yield with roughly 10-year duration, a 100bp rise in yields produces about a 10% capital loss offset by the 5% carry for a net loss of roughly 5%, meaning the higher the starting yield base, the more attractive bonds become as a holding again.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: A simple mental model for judging when higher-yield bonds re-enter 'buy' territory as an income/hedge asset after years of unattractive real returns.
insights.quote: if you've got a 5% carry, that means you're only facing a 5% uh loss overall on your total return... the higher the yield base goes, the more attractive the bond markets are.

insights.claim: Howell calls the COVID-era negative interest rate policy 'insanity,' noting that in four millennia of recorded interest-rate history (per Sydney Homer's 'A History of Interest Rates,' required reading at Salomon Brothers where Howell worked) there is no precedent for zero or negative rates, and that negative rates perversely incentivize taking on more debt -- the opposite of what the system needs.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Frames the post-2020 return to positive real/nominal rates as a reversion to historical norms rather than an aberration, reinforcing the view that the negative-rate era was itself the anomaly.
insights.quote: nowhere in that pages is there any reference at all to zero or even negative interest rates. It just didn't happen... it's a mad world because if you have negative interest rates you clearly incentivize people to take on more debt.

insights.claim: Since year 2000, Howell notes the S&P 500 is up roughly 6-7x, gold is up roughly 12-13x, and Bitcoin's gain is a further order of magnitude beyond that -- evidence he cites for the monetary-inflation-hedge thesis over multi-decade horizons.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: A long-horizon performance comparison supporting overweighting hard-asset/monetary-inflation hedges over equities as the primary store-of-wealth allocation.
insights.quote: since year 2000 I think I'm correct in saying that the S&P is up six or seven times... but the gold market is up 12 13 times and bitcoin is some magnitude more than that

insights.claim: Howell's key tail risk to the debt-refinancing/liquidity system is opaque, overlapping balance sheets from the growth of shadow banking (A lends to B, B lends to C, C lends to D, and so on), where a single failure can cascade into a multitude of interconnected failures -- the scale of this overlap is unknown but suspected to be large.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: A hidden systemic-risk vector to monitor -- interconnected non-bank lending chains -- that standard leverage metrics don't fully capture and could amplify a localized shock.
insights.quote: before you know it you get one failure and you get uh that gives rise to a multitude or or or 26 you know alphabetic failures and so the whole thing is multiplied and that that's really the risk.

insights.claim: The Federal Reserve's Standing Repo Facility, designed to backstop money markets in a crisis, has never been genuinely stress-tested, and Howell expects it will likely fail in a real crisis (as such mechanisms typically do), forcing the Fed to fall back on printing more money.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: Investors shouldn't over-rely on the SRF as a guaranteed crisis backstop; its real test is still ahead, and its likely failure mode is more, not less, monetary expansion.
insights.quote: we hope that is a good uh crisis uh protection tool. We don't know because it hasn't really been tested and the reality is that it probably will fail in a crisis because these things always do.

insights.claim: Howell states the only scenario in which his monetary-debasement thesis would prove wrong is the discovery of an entirely new way to fund government debt without printing money -- something he says has no precedent in thousands of years of financial history -- and adds that even a worst-case kinetic war scenario would still ultimately be resolved through money printing to fund the conflict.
insights.speaker: Michael Howell
insights.so_what: A clear falsifiability marker investors can use to test whether Howell's core thesis is being validated or broken over the coming years.
insights.quote: in in thousands of years of history, I mean, that's that's never appeared... financial markets now debt refinancing mechanisms and in a world of debt refinancing it's basically all about money printing and that's that's that's it
